thread.title: Apple brings some Epic Systems, Cerner medical records to iPhone

author: Elise Reuter
title: Apple brings some Epic Systems, Cerner medical records to iPhone
text: – Reporter, Kansas City Business Journal Feb 2, 2018, 10:11am CST A partnership with Apple Inc . will allow employees and clients of Epic Systems Corp. of Verona and competitors like Cerner Corp. to pull up health records on their smartphones. Last week, Apple (Nasdaq: AAPL) announced an update to its preinstalled Health app that allows users to pull in medical records from 12 different facilities. Those include Epic Systems clients like Johns Hopkins Medicine of Baltimore and Kansas City-based Cerner (Nasdaq: CERN) clients like Dignity Health and MedStar Health, as well as Cerner's onsite Healthe Clinics in the Kansas City metro. A beta test of sorts, the update marks the first time patients can pull records from different health systems into the app. Users will be able to pull in allergy information, immunization records, lab results, prescriptions, vitals and procedure details from the 12 participating facilities. To sync the data, they must login to the respective hospital or clinic's patient portal, and then link that account to Apple Health. They'll also be able to view that information alongside other metrics recorded in the app, such as steps, sleep and nutrition. "Our goal is to help consumers live a better day. We've worked closely with the health community to create an experience everyone has wanted for years — to view medical records easily and securely right on your iPhone," Apple chief operating officer Jeff Williams said in a statement. "By empowering customers to see their overall health, we hope to help consumers better understand their health and help them lead healthier lives." For Cerner employees, the partnership will mark another opportunity to access the newest health tools, said John Gresham , vice president and general manager of DeviceWorks and interoperability. Cerner hosts its Healthe Clinics at each of its campuses throughout the Kansas City metro, where employees can schedule appointments and pick up prescriptions. Now they'll be able to view that information on their iPhones. "We're excited about what this means for the community. Cerner has had a longstanding innovative relationship with our own associates," Gresham told the Kansas City Business Journal. "We're excited to be part of this living lab." While consumers have a right to their health records, in most cases, they still have to puzzle together paper records, CDs and online copies from different facilities. But recent developments in technology have the potential to change that. An open standard called FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) lets the Apple Health app "talk" to different health record systems. Because of that, hospitals on systems provided by Epic and Cerner as well as rival Athenahealth Inc. can allow patients to sync their data with Apple Health. "In general, many (people) are surprised by how hard it is … to have your health information flow seamlessly," Cerner's Gresham said. "As far as being able to have an easy secure, private method for being able to bring data down to a device for a consumer, this is fairly new to the industry." In the future, Gresham hopes more health systems will get involved. The technology also could be applied to other types of devices, too, including Android devices. Another next step will be to allow users to share health information with providers, or schedule appointments from their phones. "It will make it easier to have a choice in where you get your health, and how you consume and acquire health care," Gresham said.
